title: Model-written wrong options rarely tempt
statement: Wrong options a model writes rarely pass a judge's test of whether they would tempt a skimming reader.
example: In seven live lesson runs, the judge found 2 of 28 machine-written wrong options tempting, and none of the 14 for word meanings.
detail: A first live run produced a quick-check wrong option no reader would choose, and no check caught it, so an advisory judge question was added asking whether each wrong option would seem believable to a Grade 9 reader who skimmed, rather than obviously absurd. Across the seven later lesson runs on two texts, the quick check's 14 machine-written wrong options got 2 holds, 6 fails and 6 unsure, and the word-meaning block's 14 got 0 holds, 10 fails and 4 unsure. All 14 blocks were still marked ready, because the question cannot hold a block. The verdicts are the judge's own, with no labelled case behind them.
against: The judge's precision has not been measured: "their precision is not yet measured (v04)" (g9/transformer/v01/QA.md line 46). With no labelled cases the judge may be too strict, and the word-meaning version asks about a reader who "has not looked closely" rather than one who skimmed (g9/transformer/src/mechanics/word-in-focus.js line 87).

evidence.quote: A first live run on Othello showed two faults no check caught: a quick-check distractor no reader would choose ("he hopes to eventually become the Moor"), and "L42" written in a student paragraph.
